**Why the PDB didn't limit the rollout:**

citations.cited_text:
Pods which are deleted or unavailable due to a rolling upgrade to an application do count
against the disruption budget, but workload resources (such as Deployment and StatefulSet)
are not limited by PDBs when doing rolling upgrades. Instead, the handling of failures
during application updates is configured in the spec for the specific workload resource.

content.text: Pods which are deleted or unavailable due to a rolling upgrade to an application do count against the disruption budget, but workload resources (such as Deployment and StatefulSet) are not limited by PDBs when doing rolling upgrades. Instead, the handling of failures during application updates is configured in the spec for the specific workload resource.

So `maxUnavailable: 1` on your PDB only protects against *voluntary evictions* (like node drains or the eviction API) — it doesn't cap how many Pods a Deployment controller can take down during a rollout. In fact,

citations.cited_text:
[Involuntary disruptions](#voluntary-and-involuntary-disruptions) cannot be prevented by PDBs; however they
do count against the budget.

to the value of the `spec.replicas` key. This may not be

**Why the imagePullPolicy plugin misses the sidecar**

citations.cited_text:
### Reinvocation policy

A single ordering of mutating admissions plugins (including webhooks) does not work for all cases
(see https://issue.k8s.io/64333 as an example). A mutating webhook can add a new sub-structure
to the object (like adding a `container` to a `pod`), and other mutating plugins which have already
run may have opinions on those new structures (like setting an `imagePullPolicy` on all containers).

A mutating webhook can add a new sub-structure to the object (like adding a `container` to a `pod`), and other mutating plugins which have already run may have opinions on those new structures (like setting an `imagePullPolicy` on all containers).

If the imagePullPolicy plugin ran before your sidecar-injecting webhook, it never saw the new container.

**Fix: use reinvocationPolicy: IfNeeded**

citations.cited_text:
To allow mutating admission plugins to observe changes made by other plugins,
built-in mutating admission plugins are re-run if a mutating webhook modifies an object,
and mutating webhooks can specify a `reinvocationPolicy` to control whether they are reinvoked as well.
citations.document_title: Dynamic Admission Control > Webhook configuration > Reinvocation policy

citations.cited_text: `reinvocationPolicy` may be set to `Never` or `IfNeeded`. It defaults to `Never`.
citations.document_title: Dynamic Admission Control > Webhook configuration > Reinvocation policy

content.text: `reinvocationPolicy` may be set to `Never` or `IfNeeded`. It defaults to `Never`.

citations.document_title: Dynamic Admission Control > Webhook configuration > Reinvocation policy

content.text: `IfNeeded`: the webhook may be called again as part of the admission evaluation if the object being admitted is modified by other admission plugins after the initial webhook call.

Since the *built-in* mutating admission plugins (which is likely where imagePullPolicy defaulting happens) are automatically re-run whenever a mutating webhook modifies the object, simply having your sidecar-injecting webhook run (even without changing its own reinvocationPolicy) should trigger that built-in plugin to re-run and set `imagePullPolicy` on the new sidecar. kind: MutatingWebhookConfiguration
```yaml
webhooks:
- name: my-webhook.example.com
  reinvocationPolicy: IfNeeded
```

and potentially modified.

### Jobs with sidecar containers

If you define a Job that uses sidecar using Kubernetes-style init containers,
the sidecar container in each Pod does not prevent the Job from completing after the
main container has finished.

content.text: If you define a Job that uses sidecar using Kubernetes-style init containers, the sidecar container in each Pod does not prevent the Job from completing after the main container has finished.

## How to declare it

Define the sidecar under `initContainers` with `restartPolicy: Always`, and keep the main logic in `containers`. Example:

```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: myjob
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: myjob
          image: alpine:latest
          command: ['sh', '-c', 'echo "logging" > /opt/logs.txt']
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /opt
      initContainers:
        - name: logshipper
          image: alpine:latest
          # Setting restartPolicy: Always makes this a sidecar container.
          restartPolicy: Always
          command: ['sh', '-c', 'tail -F /opt/logs.txt']
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /opt
      restartPolicy: Never
      volumes:
        - name: data
          emptyDir: {}
```

citations.cited_text:
##### Restart behavior comparison

The following table shows how containers behave under different restart policies and exit codes:

| Exit Code | `restartPolicy: Always` | `restartPolicy: OnFailure` | `restartPolicy: Never` | Sidecar Containers |
|-----------|-------------------------|---------------------------|------------------------|-------------------|
| 0 (Success) | Restarts | Does not restart | Does not restart | Always restarts |
| Non-zero (Failure) | Restarts | Restarts | Does not restart | Always restarts |

**Note:** The restart behavior is particularly important when choosing between Deployments and Jobs:
- **Deployments** typically use `restartPolicy: Always` (the only allowed value) to keep applications running continuously
- **Jobs** commonly use `restartPolicy: OnFailure` or `restartPolicy: Never` to handle batch processing tasks appropriately
- **Sidecar containers** are init containers that always restart regardless of the Pod's `restartPolicy` because they have their own container-level `restartPolicy: Always`

```yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1

metadata:

spec:

    spec:
      restartPolicy: OnFailure  # Only restart on non-zero exit codes
      containers:
      - name: processor
        image: busybox:1.28
        command: ['sh', '-c', 'echo "Processing data..."; exit 0']
```

## How it works

citations.cited_text:
### TTL mechanism for finished Jobs

Feature state: `Kubernetes v1.23 [stable]`

Another way to clean up finished Jobs (either `Complete` or `Failed`)
automatically is to use a TTL mechanism provided by a
[TTL controller](/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/ttlafterfinished/) for
finished resources, by specifying the `.spec.ttlSecondsAfterFinished` field of
the Job.
citations.document_title: Jobs > Clean up finished jobs automatically > TTL mechanism for finished Jobs

content.text: Another way to clean up finished Jobs (either `Complete` or `Failed`) automatically is to use a TTL mechanism provided by a TTL controller for finished resources, by specifying the `.spec.ttlSecondsAfterFinished` field of the Job.

citations.cited_text:
The TTL-after-finished controller assumes that a Job is eligible to be cleaned up
TTL seconds after the Job has finished. The timer starts once the
status condition of the Job changes to show that the Job is either `Complete` or `Failed`; once the TTL has
expired, that Job becomes eligible for
[cascading](/docs/concepts/architecture/garbage-collection/#cascading-deletion) removal.

Importantly,

citations.cited_text:
When the TTL controller cleans up the Job, it will delete the Job cascadingly,
i.e. delete its dependent objects, such as Pods, together with the Job.

The `NetworkPolicyPeer` fields available are only `ipBlock`, `namespaceSelector`, and `podSelector`, and these describe traffic to **allow**:

citations.cited_text:
## NetworkPolicyPeer

NetworkPolicyPeer describes a peer to allow traffic to/from. Only certain combinations of fields are allowed

- `ipBlock` *[IPBlock](/docs/reference/kubernetes-api/networking/#IPBlock)*: ipBlock defines policy on a particular IPBlock.
citations.document_title: NetworkPolicy > NetworkPolicyPeer

content.text: NetworkPolicyPeer describes a peer to allow traffic to/from. Only certain combinations of fields are allowed - `ipBlock` *IPBlock*: ipBlock defines policy on a particular IPBlock.

There's no deny-rule mechanism — NetworkPolicy is purely additive/allow-based.

**What you can do instead:**

Kubernetes NetworkPolicy works by isolating pods with a default-deny policy, then explicitly allowing what you want. There's no direct "deny this one namespace" primitive, but you can achieve an equivalent effect using an "allow everything except X" pattern via `namespaceSelector` combined with the immutable namespace-name label.

Kubernetes automatically labels namespaces with a name label you can select against:

citations.cited_text:
## Targeting a Namespace by its name

The Kubernetes control plane sets an immutable label `kubernetes.io/metadata.name` on all
namespaces, the value of the label is the namespace name.

While NetworkPolicy cannot target a namespace by its name with some object field, you can use the
standardized label to target a specific namespace.
citations.document_title: Network Policies > Targeting a Namespace by its name

content.text: The Kubernetes control plane sets an immutable label `kubernetes.io/metadata.name` on all namespaces, the value of the label is the namespace name. While NetworkPolicy cannot target a namespace by its name with some object field, you can use the standardized label to target a specific namespace.

Since `namespaceSelector` uses standard label selector semantics, you can use a `NotIn` match expression to select "all namespaces except the one you want to block":

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-all-except-one-namespace
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchExpressions:
        - key: kubernetes.io/metadata.name
          operator: NotIn
          values:
          - blocked-namespace
```

This relies on the fact that

citations.cited_text: - `namespaceSelector` *[LabelSelector](/docs/reference/kubernetes-api/definitions/label-selector-v1-meta/#LabelSelector)*: namespaceSelector selects namespaces using cluster-scoped labels. To block all outgoing traffic from pods in a namespace, create a NetworkPolicy that selects all pods but allows no egress:

```yaml
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-egress
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
```

citations.cited_text:
### Default deny all egress traffic

You can create a "default" egress isolation policy for a namespace by creating a NetworkPolicy
that selects all pods but does not allow any egress traffic from those pods.

Example file `service/networking/network-policy-default-deny-egress.yaml`:

```yaml
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-egress
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
```

This ensures that even pods that aren't selected by any other NetworkPolicy will not be allowed
egress traffic.
citations.document_title: Network Policies > Default policies > Default deny all egress traffic

content.text: You can create a "default" egress isolation policy for a namespace by creating a NetworkPolicy that selects all pods but does not allow any egress traffic from those pods. This ensures that even pods that aren't selected by any other NetworkPolicy will not be allowed egress traffic.
This does not affect ingress:

citations.cited_text: This policy does not change the ingress isolation behavior of any pod.
citations.document_title: Network Policies > Default policies > Default deny all egress traffic

content.text: This policy does not change the ingress isolation behavior of any pod.
**Why DNS breaks:**

citations.cited_text:
**Caution:** A default deny-all egress policy also blocks DNS traffic. If your workloads need DNS
resolution, you must add a separate NetworkPolicy that allows egress to your
cluster's DNS service.
citations.document_title: Network Policies > Default policies > Default deny all egress traffic

content.text: A default deny-all egress policy also blocks DNS traffic. If your workloads need DNS resolution, you must add a separate NetworkPolicy that allows egress to your cluster's DNS service.

This happens because Pod DNS lookups are themselves outbound network requests (typically UDP/TCP to the cluster DNS service), and since the policy denies *all* egress by default, those DNS queries get blocked along with everything else — there's no automatic exception for DNS.

**Fix:** Add an additional NetworkPolicy permitting egress to your DNS service/pods (e.g., allowing egress to the `kube-system` namespace or the specific DNS pod/port, typically UDP/TCP 53), alongside your deny-all-egress policy.

Set `clusterIP: None` on the Service that the StatefulSet's `serviceName` points to. For example:

```yaml

metadata:
  name: mysql
  labels:
    app: mysql
    app.kubernetes.io/name: mysql
spec:
  ports:
  - name: mysql
    port: 3306
  clusterIP: None
  selector:
    app: mysql
```
